https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/toi-.text: Welcome back to another edition of My Take 5. This week we are covering several related developments linked to Ukraine â Jared Kushner & Steve Witkoffâs visit to Kyiv, Modiâs appeal to Putin, Latviaâs mulling of tariffs against Russian grain â the far-right AfDâs stunning victory in a German state election, and UK along with a host of other countries sanctioning Israeli settlements in the West Bank. So, letâs get to it.Kushner & Witkoff in Kyiv: In a bid to restart peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, Trumpâs envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Moscow and Kyiv this past weekend. The Kyiv visit, astonishingly, was their first in the entire duration of Russiaâs full-scale war against Ukraine. Both of them, of course, have been to Moscow multiple times. This tells you something about their priorities. Nonetheless, the fact that they finally made it to Kyiv is still significant. But their meeting with Putin in Moscow, according to reports, showed little inclination on the Russian leaderâs part to end the war. In fact, Putin reportedly told the envoys that Russia was in a âstrong positionâ on the battlefield, and that the war would continue until Russiaâs core objectives were achieved. There was also the hackneyed reference to resolving Russiaâs âcore issuesâ (cue the eye-roll) to end the war.Of course, Putin is window dressing the situation for the Americans. Things are actually not so rosy for the Russians with Ukraine stepping up its drone strikes against Russian military and military-support targets deep inside Russian territory. This has included, as is well known by now, strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, military-industrial plants, and large commercial warehouses of Wildberries and Ozon that store and supply military equipment. The Ukrainian strikes have been extensive, reaching almost all corners of Russia.Meanwhile, the situation on the battlefront hasnât changed much. Russian forces are moving at their slowest pace since the start of the full-scale invasion, and the Ukrainian army is not only holding firm but also launching its own counterattacks.But given Putinâs projection of the situation, itâs clear that Moscow is willing to continue the war and drag it into yet another winter, which will be very difficult for Ukraine. Hence, when Kushner and Witkoff landed in Kyiv, they discussed with Zelenskyy the winter support package that Ukraine desperately needs for the coming months, and the supply of missile interceptors to protect Ukrainian cities.So, the only progress from the twin trips is that there is an in-principle agreement to restart trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia that had halted earlier this year when US launched its own war against Iran. But even the previous iteration of the talks produced little progress towards a ceasefire, much less a peace deal. Hence, itâs unlikely that the resumption of the talks this time will produce anything different, especially since Putin remains adamant on continuing the war. Ukraine, therefore, needs all the international support it can get for the upcoming winter. And perhaps, just perhaps, Kushner and Witkoff may finally impress on Trump the truth that is plain for everyone â it is Putin that doesnât want to put a stop to this senseless, illegal war.Modiâs appeal to Putin: The Kushner-Witkoff visit to Kyiv came days after Modi told Putin that one had to move from endless war to end of war, on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. This isnât the first time Modi has told Putin to end Russiaâs war against Ukraine. On previous occasions he had told Putin that this isnât an era of war. But the Russian leader clearly isnât listening to Modi. In fact, just after Modiâs latest appeal to Putin, foreign minister S Jaishankar made his first solo visit to Ukraine where he stuck to Modiâs formulation of ending the war and offering Indiaâs help in this regard.So, taken together, India and other countries have told Putin to end his war against Ukraine, but they havenât been successful in convincing him. This is because Putin wants to continue this war and is willing to expend many more Russian men and materiel to achieve his so-called objectives. Again, nice words wonât change Putinâs mind. Real sanctions and pressure are the only things that can work.Latvia plans tariffs on Russian-Belarussian grain: The Baltic countries totally get the above point, and are acutely aware of the threat Russia can pose to them. Therefore, they have been staunch supporters of Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression. Now, Latviaâs government is planning to impose 300% tariff on grain arriving from Russia and its ally Belarus. In fact, last week both Latvia and Lithuania considered ending transshipment of Russian grain through their ports. In fact, Russia has been moving grain through Latvia to other markets in response to Ukraineâs retaliatory strikes on Russiaâs shipping routes through Black Sea and Azov Sea â Russia has been persistently striking Ukrainian ports like that in Odesa and other Ukrainian shipping infra.Thus, if Latvia goes ahead with its high tariff wall for Russian grain, it will cut off a key alternative route for Moscow and put pressure on the Russian economy.German far-right AfD wins provincial elections: In a big jolt to German politics, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won the elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. However, AfD fell just short of majority that would have guaranteed the first far-right German state government since World War II. Now AfD has to form a coalition if it wants to govern in the province. Nonetheless, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the development a big challenge to German politics that âchanges all of Germanyâ. Reports indicate that AfD rode to victory on resentment with the Merz federal government, populist narratives against immigrants, and Euro-scepticism. Apparently, there are young German people who feel that leaders in Berlin are not responsive to their concerns, feelings that have been accentuated by Germanyâs economic slowdown in recent years. However, this year, the German economy is looking strong and is forecast to grow by 1.3% or more.Clearly, the AfD preyed on grievances of those disaffected with the federal government and made immigrants and EUâs immigration policies the scapegoat. But the real threat of AfDâs rise is to the EU itself. Germany is the engine of the European bloc. If it takes a hard-right political turn, it could lead to an implosion of the EU from within. There are two forces today who actually want that â Trump and Putin. Trump, because he sees the EU and its liberal values as a challenge to his own MAGA politics in the US. Thatâs why MAGA allies like Elon Musk have been rooting for AfD. Putin, of course, wants the EU gone because it stands in the way of Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine, and broader plans to increase Russiaâs expansion â both through physical presence and influence â across parts of Europe. And many AfD leaders have open connections with Putin.So, it makes one wonder: Have the US and Russia, separately but simultaneously, been peddling propaganda that influence German voters and shore up AfDâs anti-immigrant, anti-EU narrative? Possibly yes. After Hungary voted out Viktor Orban earlier this year, EU was celebrating that election as a vindication of European values. But the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt presents a new challenge to the European bloc.UK sanctions Israeli settlements: In a big move UK announced sanctions against Israeli settlements in Palestinian West Bank. These Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. UK government said that it will introduce an import ban on goods from these settlements and join similar moves by France and Canada. Plus, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden have pledged to support further action in this direction.The move comes as Israeli settlers have increasingly tried to muscle their way into Palestinian land and property in the West Bank in recent months, even occupying Palestinian homes. This has even seen US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemn the militant settlers who have been seizing private property in West Bank villages such as Qusra. The settlers also laid siege to the home of one Palestinian American.But it remains to be seen if any of this will have an impact on the Netanyahu government as it prepares for elections in Israel. In fact, international sanctions against the settlements could actually rally Israeli right-wing groups. The fact remains that these settlers are emboldened only because they know the Israeli government and army are with them. Therefore, the nub of the issue lies in Tel Aviv.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Cop31 Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said. But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether the world’s countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month. Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps. Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia – which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31 – pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations. View image in fullscreen Fijian dancers perform at the summit’s welcome ceremony. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific. But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and Europe , representatives from big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders. On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu , a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival. In a powerful speech, the 13-year-old Melelusi Sokotia told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”. Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”. “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight,” Tabuya said. “Our responsibility does not.” View image in fullscreen Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya (centre) reacts during the summit’s closing session on Thursday. Photograph: Pacific pre-Cop31/AFP/Getty Images The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C , well beyond the 1.5C goal of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses. Through the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for the poor and vulnerable who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised. Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal Read more Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31 .” Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk. Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.” View image in fullscreen Leaders attend a session at the summit. Photograph: Getty Images “The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%. But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed. Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago . But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels. View image in fullscreen Chris Bowen, a Cop31 president-designate and Australia’s climate minister, chairs a session on Thursday. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel, but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants. Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil . Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya. Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout. “This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.” Explore more on these topics Cop31 Climate crisis Turkey Fiji Asia Pacific Tuvalu Pacific islands news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
